prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which many atoms held at a magic wavelength allow frequency standards of unprecedented precision

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for B049, Katori and Ye. After the full first-round exchange the scientific case looks to me stronger, not weaker. The central idea is a mechanism, not a better number: a lattice light field tuned to the magic wavelength shifts both clock levels equally, so thousands of neutral atoms are held without Doppler or recoil broadening and without a trap-induced line shift. That removes the old trade-off between atom number and perturbation that limited single-ion clocks to the signal-to-noise of one particle. It is a statement about how nature allows an ensemble to be made clean, and it was not obvious in advance. It is mature in the sense I care most about as a theorist: every systematic shift (blackbody, polarisability, hyperpolarisability, density-dependent collisions) is understood quantitatively and the theory agrees with the measurements; uncertainties near 1e-18 are reached in several laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA/NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others) and clocks are compared across sites and continents. On credit, Katori made the proposal and the first realisation. Ye's group showed that the scheme survives at the 1e-18 level and, importantly, that interactions and many-body effects in the lattice can be understood and controlled, which is what turned the idea into a working frontier instrument and revealed physics (collective and density-dependent shifts, spin-exchange interactions) of its own. I would therefore keep both names, with a citation confined to the invention and realisation and no list of applications, so that the prize is not read as a lifetime award for precision metrology.
statement.case_against: The strongest objections remain, and I do not think they are fully answered. First, overlap with 2005 (Hall and Hansch, frequency comb) and 2012 (Wineland and Haroche, control of single quantum systems and ion clocks): a committee could still say this is the next clock in a recognised lineage. My answer is that those prizes honoured the ruler and the control of single quantum objects, whereas the lattice clock rests on a separate idea, but that is an argument and not a proof. Second, the discovery content: no departure from known physics has been seen (no drift of constants, no dark-matter signal), so this is an enabling measurement capability and not a new phenomenon, and the geodesy and constants-test harvest is partly prospective. Third, Ye's share is the weakest link in the two-name credit; if the committee judges that performance and many-body refinement are execution of Katori's idea, a Katori-only prize would be the purist outcome, and Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto, Lisdat, Ludlow and others remain outside the credit.

responses.point: Olsson accepts Katori's clean priority but questions whether Ye's contribution is part of the invention and realisation or a later, much better execution, and asks whether the prize would still stand with Katori alone.
responses.response: Yes, I think a Katori-only prize would stand scientifically, and I want to be honest that this is the real fault line. My reason for keeping Ye is that he did not only improve a number. The question after the proposal was whether a lattice with thousands of atoms could really reach the 1e-18 regime, since collisional and many-body effects might have spoiled it, and the JILA work answered that by identifying and controlling density-dependent and interaction shifts, which is the part of this field that a theorist finds most interesting. That is part of realising the scheme, not a lifetime award. I accept Olsson's discipline on the citation: it should say invention and realisation, name the magic-wavelength lattice and not enumerate precision records, and the record should state that the clock work, not Ye's frequency-comb or molecular work, is what is credited. If colleagues judge that Ye's share does not meet that bar, I would accept a reduction to Katori alone before I would add a name from outside the shortlisted credit.

responses.point: Pearce moved B049 to the centre of a two-part proposal and pairs it with B047 (Halzen alone, IceCube high-energy astrophysical neutrinos), while conceding that the single-name credit is the weakest point and that the second part is droppable.
responses.response: I thank Pearce for the clear disclosure and for saying he would fall back to B049 alone. I remain unable to support B047 as a second part, for the reason he himself gives: nothing in the supplied credit lets me show that one person carries the discovery of a diffuse flux seen by a collaboration of hundreds, and the source identifications rest on one instrument. This is a field where I defer to the astroparticle members, and none of them has put forward a defensible one-to-three-name attribution, so I would not add a part whose credit is conceded to be weak merely to make a two-part prize. A single-achievement prize is, to my mind, the more honest outcome when only one candidate has both secure science and a compact credit. If a colleague can supply a documented broader set of names for IceCube, I would listen, but under the three-person limit that would also squeeze the clock credit.

responses.point: Kroll, who ranked B049 first, stresses that independent confirmation by several laboratories is the evidence, and that the scientific harvest (second redefinition, geodesy at scale, constants tests, dark-matter limits) is partly still prospective.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of Kroll's argument and I now state it more sharply than in round one: the maturity of B049 does not rest on the harvest. It rests on a measured quantity that independent groups reproduce and cross-compare, and on theory that accounts for each shift. I would therefore keep geodesy, constants tests and the redefinition of the second out of the citation, and treat them as consequences. That also answers the chair's question on whether this is a discovery or an instrument: it is a discovery about what a trapped neutral-atom ensemble allows, and I do not need an anomaly to justify it. I concede to Kroll, who initially hesitated on this, that if the committee demands a measured departure from known physics as the test for discovery, B049 fails that test and so do most metrology prizes.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B024 (theta-13 from reactor antineutrinos) as a clean decisive measurement, but acknowledges that only two members ranked it in the top eight and that the committee may legitimately move toward B049 or B048.
responses.response: I respect Danielsson's candour about breadth of support, and as a theorist I find theta-13 an attractive example of a parameter nature had to supply. My reservations are unchanged and are about credit, not quality: Daya Bay, RENO and Double Chooz were near-simultaneous, three spokesperson names cannot represent them or the accelerator appearance results, and the 2015 oscillation prize already honoured the phenomenon. I do not know the internal leadership history well enough to settle whether Luk, Kim and Wang are the right three, and Danielsson himself lists this as a risk. That is why I keep B024 out of my alternatives, while taking seriously his point that it is experimentally secure. I would take B048 ahead of it if B049 does not carry, since there the committee has a more compact theory-plus-experiment story.

responses.point: Eriksson alone prefers B048 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp), the time-reversal-invariant topological insulator and quantum spin Hall effect, as a single-part prize with a compound theory-plus-experiment citation.
responses.response: Eriksson's configuration is the strongest fallback I can see: a prediction followed by a direct experimental realisation, which is the pattern I trust. This is condensed-matter physics, where I defer, and my question is the one in the chair's summary: the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who proposed the HgTe realisation, makes the credit contestable, and I do not know how firmly edge-conductance quantisation has been reproduced outside the Molenkamp group. That is why I do not rank it above B049, but I have moved B048 into my alternatives in place of B044, because trapped-ion quantum computing competes with B054 for the same theorists (Cirac, Zoller) and splits support, while B048 is a distinct achievement with a more compact credit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 precision-measurement prizes; this is argument, and I cannot settle it from the record.

Whether Ye's contribution is part of the invention and realisation or later execution, and so whether Katori alone would be the more defensible attribution; I rely on memory for priority and have not checked the primary papers.
Whether other contributors outside the two names (Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto, Lisdat, Ludlow) have claims that the citation can fairly omit.

Whether the committee prefers a single-part prize to a two-part prize when the second part has only a weak attribution; I defer to astroparticle colleagues on whether any IceCube credit can be documented.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Katori or Ye. I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, and I know the precision atomic-structure community, but none of these people is a candidate on the shortlist and I do not request recusal on any shortlisted ballot. I record the connections for transparency and would recuse if a candidate from among my own collaborators were considered.
